findings.what: close() restores the interrupt flag in the finally around the join, which runs BEFORE failAll(drainRemaining()) and delegate.close(). The round-3 fix moved the defect one statement later rather than closing it: the join now waits, but the delegate -- the LocalSequencer whose close() is the lease release -- is entered with the interrupt flag set. LeaseManager.release() falls through to BoundedLock.takeOrFail whenever tryLock() loses to an in-flight renew, and takeOrFail's ReentrantLock.tryLock(timeout) throws InterruptedException IMMEDIATELY when the flag is already set. The JDK's own ExecutorService.close() puts the restore as its LAST statement for exactly this reason; here there is real, interruptible I/O after it.
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED on the staged bytes, in a copy of the index. A BatchingSequencer over a delegate whose close() models LeaseManager.release (tryLock, then a bounded tryLock(5s)), with a renew holding the lease lock, closed from a thread that already carries an interrupt -- the shutdown path this method's own comment names as hitting 'every time'. Result: interruptAtDelegateClose=true leaseReleased=false closeThrew='interrupted waiting for the lease lock to release' flagStillSet=true. So the lease is NOT released and leadership only moves when the TTL expires -- the ~10 s failover the class javadoc and closingWithACallerParkedFailsItAndClosesTheDelegate both say close() exists to avoid -- and close() throws IOException, so anything the caller's shutdown sequence does after it is skipped. Moving the restore into a finally around delegate.close() flips it: interruptAtDelegateClose=false leaseReleased=true closeThrew=none flagStillSet=true, i.e. the caller still gets its interrupt back. Note the wider reachability too: any store backend whose PUT is interrupt-sensitive (ClosedByInterruptException, which this file's own drain-loop comment cites) aborts the lease release on this path without needing lock contention at all.

findings.what: Dead code left by the file split, unchanged since round 3: the private record ClosingSequencer is declared here and used only in BatchingSequencerLifecycleTest (where it is a second, identical copy), and commitConcurrently's QueuedTimer parameter (line 88) is never read in the method body.
findings.failure_scenario: No runtime failure. It costs a reader: the next person to add a lifecycle test to this file reads ClosingSequencer as an in-use fixture, and the unread timer parameter reads as a synchronisation dependency the method does not have -- which is precisely the kind of misreading that produced the latch-based window fixture the file's own comments say cost 2 PUTs where 1 was demanded.

findings.what: The committer's own death is still unlogged. close()'s new WARNING covers only the join timeout; the drainLoop catch(Throwable) path -- a WindowTimer throw, an Error out of the delegate -- fails the held callers with the cause, shuts the door, and returns without a single log line. Later callers then get IOException('this sequencer is closed'), which is indistinguishable from an orderly shutdown.
findings.failure_scenario: A LinkageError from a lazily-loaded store SDK class, or an OOM in the encode, kills the committer at 03:00. The in-flight caller sees the Error; every caller after it sees 'this sequencer is closed' and the operator's logs say the sequencer was closed -- which it was not, by anyone. Diagnosis starts from the wrong hypothesis (a deliberate shutdown) with nothing in the log naming the batcher's permanent death or its cause.
